node.label: Gayle S. Rubin
node.date_label: The Traffic in Women (1975) · Thinking Sex (1984) · Sexual Traffic, with Judith Butler (1994) · Deviations (2011)
node.description: In “The Traffic in Women” (1975), Gayle S. Rubin argued that women’s subordination requires analysis of a sex/gender system: social arrangements that organize sexuality and produce gendered positions. In “Thinking Sex” (1984), Rubin distinguished sexual stratification from gender hierarchy and called for their separate analysis. These interventions became major resources for feminist and queer scholarship. Butler explicitly credited the first essay’s account of gender’s mobility as one reason for developing Gender Trouble (1990). The framework also attracted criticism: in her Stanford Encyclopedia entry, Mari Mikkola summarizes her own 2011 objection to the sex/gender distinction underlying accounts such as Rubin’s. Treating gender as socially constructed suggests that women and men could cease to exist if social practices changed; treating gender as a product of oppression further suggests that feminism should seek that outcome. Mikkola regards these commitments as politically unhelpful, particularly because many people value their gender. In the 1994 Butler interview, Rubin described the later essay as a correction addressing different problems and rejected an exclusive disciplinary division between feminism and sexuality studies. Deviations (2011) collected the major essays alongside further work on sexual politics, history and knowledge.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “The Traffic in Women: Notes on the ‘Political Economy’ of Sex” (1975); “Thinking Sex: Notes for a Radical Theory of the Politics of Sexuality” (1984); “Sexual Traffic,” interview with Judith Butler (1994; Portuguese journal translation 2003); Deviations: A Gayle Rubin Reader (2011, collection).
node.scope_note: The two major essays were not read on a permitted route; they are represented through Rubin’s 1994 interview, Mikkola’s SEP entry and the Duke description. The 1994 interview was read in selected passages of its 2003 Portuguese journal translation; English body unread. Deviations was checked through its catalogue, contents and displayed openings, not read as a whole. Mikkola’s separate 2011 article and the cited theorists’ original books remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin recalls that reading Lévi-Strauss’s The Elementary Structures of Kinship transformed her thinking and fed into “The Traffic in Women” (1975).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. JSTOR chapter and the 1975 anthology on Internet Archive are access-restricted). The interview supports the debt half only: Lévi-Strauss's Elementary Structures fed 'The Traffic in Women'. Re-base as influence; restore the critique only if the essay can be read on a permitted route. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"Sahlins sugeriu que eu lesse Estruturas Elementares do Parentesco, de Lévi-Strauss. Para usar a linguagem da época, 'o livro fez minha cabeça'"; "'The Traffic in Women' foi o resultado da confluência desses estudos"”

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin recalls concluding that Marxism, though useful, could not account for gender difference and women’s oppression, the problem “The Traffic in Women” (1975) set out to address.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The interview supports a critique of the explanatory limits of Marxism (not specifically Marx's labour-power account) as the problem the essay addressed. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"O marxismo ... parecia incapaz de entender os temas da diferença de gênero e da opressão das mulheres"; "[o paradigma marxista] era útil, mas ao mesmo tempo tinha limitações no que diz respeito a gênero e sexo"; "'Traffic in Women' foi parte desse esforço"”
proposed_edges.map_label: Marxism’s limits on gender and sex

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin describes Lacanian psychoanalysis as a tool that was “very useful” for analysing structures of gender and desire in her work, while objecting to its totalizing tendencies and non-social conception of the symbolic.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. In the interview (GR answer after Butler's Gender Trouble remark), Rubin describes Lacanian psychoanalysis as a useful tool with reservations. This supports a qualified influence. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"a psicanálise lacaniana constituía uma ferramenta para isso"; "muito útil para lidar com estruturas de gênero e desejo, mas tem seu preço. Eu me preocupava com as tendências totalizantes em Lacan"”

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin says that Foucault’s History of Sexuality (English 1978) clarified issues and inspired the work behind “Thinking Sex” (1984), which had begun before she read it; she adds that Jeffrey Weeks influenced her as much.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The interview gives Rubin's own stated debt to Foucault for the Thinking Sex work, with the caveat that the work predated her reading. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"o trabalho começou antes que eu começasse a ler Foucault, mas o livro dele esclareceu alguns temas e me inspirou"; History of Sexuality "Foi um livro muito importante"; "Fui influenciada por Weeks da mesma forma que por Foucault"”

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Butler credits Rubin’s “The Traffic in Women” (1975) as one reason for developing Gender Trouble (1990).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Portuguese translation (2003), JB paragraph beginning E o que me interessou, ending developed “Gender Trouble” (HTML lines 118–119): “um dos motivos”. Explicit first-person debt concerning gender’s mobility; English interview and Gender Trouble unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin credits Althusser’s “Freud and Lacan” (English 1969) in the formation of “The Traffic in Women” (1975).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Portuguese translation, GR paragraph beginning Li o artigo de Althusser (HTML line 92): “confluência desses estudos”. English publication year from interview bibliography; does not date the French original. Althusser essay unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sexual Traffic” (1994), Rubin recalls that Charles Tilly’s 1973 Michigan course on the urbanization of Europe changed her thinking and led her to ask how forms of sexual identity arose from the same large-scale social changes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. The interview independently supports a teaching debt to Tilly, located in Rubin's history of sexual identity rather than in the 1984 acknowledgment. The interview translation is published by the journal (Cadernos Pagu 21, 2003, DOI 10.1590/S0104-83332003000200008) with the note 'Entrevista © Gayle Rubin', so I treat it as an authorised journal translation (a coordinator may confirm). Quotations are Portuguese; English renderings are mine. Phrase seen: “"Em 1973, fiz outro curso que mudou minha vida 'A urbanização da Europa, 1500-1900', ministrado por Charles Tilly"; from these questions "a pensar em como diferentes formas de identidade e de subjetividade sexual resultaram das mesmas mudanças sociais em larga escala, foi um passo"”

proposed_edges.relationship: “The Traffic in Women” (1975) supplied a sex/gender-system framework for explaining women’s subordination through social relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mikkola, section 1.2, paragraphs naming Rubin (1975), describes the framework and social production of gender; Duke describes feminist reception. A theoretical contribution to the gender-history field, not a claim that Rubin founded that field.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Thinking Sex” (1984) set out to treat oppression based on sexual behaviour as distinct from gender oppression and to make structures of sexual stratification visible, as Rubin explains in “Sexual Traffic” (1994); Duke University Press calls it one of queer theory’s foundational texts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on gr_w_interview_1994; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. Rubin's own interview account and the Duke description support the claim; 'historical analysis' is not stated in either, so dropped. 1984 is confirmed by the interview bibliography (Vance, Pleasure and Danger, 1984). Phrase seen: “"eu queria ser capaz de pensar sobre a opressão com base no comportamento sexual ou no desejo ilícito como algo distinto da opressão de gênero"; "articular as estruturas da estratificação sexual e torná-las visíveis"; Duke: "That essay became one of queer theory's foundational texts"”

proposed_edges.relationship: As Clyde Plumauzille documents, Rubin’s The Traffic in Women (1975) was among the critical resources Joan Wallach Scott attended to in seeking an approach beyond the category of woman and economic or familial explanations of women’s subordination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Substantive intellectual history in the Institute’s own magazine. This is Plumauzille’s account, not Scott’s stated debt; it supports a specific resource, not sole causation. Scott’s 1986 article itself was not readable at the JSTOR page checked.
proposed_edges.map_label: A resource for Scott’s methodological shift

proposed_edges.relationship: In Changing Hands (2013), Sara Ahmed draws on Rubin’s account in Deviations (2011) of gender circulating through conversations to argue against treating concepts as isolated individual inventions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Ahmed’s own published presentation. Her response develops Rubin’s atmospheric account into an argument about collective conceptual production. Ahmed cites a 2012 edition; the publisher dates the original collection to November 2011. Full collection unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the English version of Gender for a Marxist Dictionary (1991), Donna Haraway argues that Rubin’s The Traffic in Women (1975), alongside Rich’s and Wittig’s formulations, made racialized gender relations and barriers to interracial feminist solidarity difficult for white feminists to grasp.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Haraway’s substantive discussion in a licensed Routledge preview. The criticism encompasses three formulations; it is not exclusively directed at Rubin. English text dated 1991 in the reprint; no complete-book reading claimed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Racial limits of the sex/gender framework

row.context: The sex/gender-system framework treats women’s subordination as socially organized; later critics question its assumptions and political implications.
Analyzes sexual stratification and its historical organization while distinguishing it from gender hierarchy.
